Identification through heteroskedasticity (Rigobon 2003), two regimes

Source: R/id-extra.R
id_hetero.Rd

With two covariance regimes \(\Sigma_1=PP'\) and \(\Sigma_2=P\Lambda P'\), \(\Lambda=\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_K)\) with distinct elements, \(P\) is identified up to column order and sign: with \(\Sigma_1=L_1L_1'\), take the eigendecomposition \(L_1^{-1}\Sigma_2L_1^{-T}=V\Lambda V'\), \(P=L_1V\). Shocks are ordered by decreasing \(\lambda_j\) (relative variance in regime 2), signs chosen so \(\mathrm{diag}(P)>0\). The result is a point impact matrix (\(\Sigma\) from the full sample need not equal \(PP'\); \(P\) satisfies it for the regime-1 covariance), returned as an id_given() object with attribute lambda. It does not propagate sampling uncertainty (all draws share one P).

Usage

id_hetero(fit, regime)

Arguments

fit

a varm() fit.

regime

logical or 0/1/2 vector of length nrow(fit$Y), TRUE/2 = regime 2.

Details

Economic intuition. Useful when volatility shifts (Great Moderation, crisis episodes, announcement days) are plausibly shock-specific, with no need for any economic restriction; the shocks are statistical and must be labelled afterwards. Pitfalls: needs distinct variance ratios (weak identification otherwise), regimes known/exogenous, and constant \(P\) across regimes.

See also

Other identification: id_proxy(), id_restrictions(), id_zerosign(), identification, irf_fry_pagan(), proxy_draws()

Examples

fit <- varm(yraw, p = 1)
regime <- rep(0:1, length.out = nrow(yraw))
id_hetero(fit, regime)
#> <varm_id> user-supplied impact matrix P (response x shock)
#>        infl  unemp   rate
#> infl  0.192 -0.288 -0.146
#> unemp 0.140  0.273 -0.241
#> rate  0.476 -0.229  0.668
